planting.note: Plant large bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; Early Fantasy opens its whorl of bells noticeably ahead of most crown imperial cultivars, extending the start of the bloom season.

directions: Plant the large bulb on its side 6-8 inches deep in fertile, sharply drained soil, since the hollow-crowned bulb rots quickly if water collects around it standing upright. Early Fantasy carries rich apricot, bell-shaped flowers on dark stems, opening noticeably earlier in the spring sequence than most crown imperial selections, which lets it bridge the gap between late daffodils and the main flush of tulips. Like other crown imperials, the whole plant has a musky scent that most gardeners find unpleasant at close range but that usefully discourages deer and voles from grazing nearby bulbs. Let the foliage yellow and collapse naturally after bloom, and avoid dividing or moving the clump, since established crown imperials resent root disturbance.

planting.note: Plant bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; Red Beauty is a scarlet-red selection with red-tinged foliage, somewhat shorter than many crown imperial cultivars.

directions: Plant the large bulb on its side 6-8 inches deep in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade, since water pooling in the hollow-crowned bulb invites rot. Red Beauty produces scarlet-red, bell-shaped flowers held beneath a tuft of red-tinged foliage on dark stems, slightly more compact than taller crown imperial cultivars, which makes it easier to place in a mixed border without it towering over neighboring bulbs. The musky, skunk-like odor of the whole plant deters deer and other browsers while adding little to its appeal up close. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering and avoid disturbing the bulb once it is established.

planting.note: Plant bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; Sunset pairs warm orange flowers with unusual burgundy-bronze foliage and stems.

directions: Plant the large bulb on its side 6-8 inches deep in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade. Sunset combines warm, sunset-orange bells with unusually dark burgundy-bronze foliage and stems, a richer contrast than the plain green stems of most crown imperial cultivars, making the whole flower stalk ornamental rather than just the blooms. The characteristic musky, skunk-like scent of the plant makes it an effective deer and vole deterrent for nearby bulbs. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back completely before cutting it away, and leave the clump undisturbed once established, since crown imperials resent being moved or divided.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun; Green Dreams bears a muted mix of dark purple and chartreuse-green florets up and down a tall, sturdy spike.

directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun, since Fritillaria persica dislikes wet, heavy ground. Green Dreams carries up to thirty small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers along a stiff, dark spike, each bloom a muted blend of dusky purple and chartreuse green that gives the whole spire an unusual smoky quality rather than the solid plum color of the typical species. Flowers open sequentially from the bottom of the spike upward over several weeks in mid to late spring, extending the display far longer than most spring bulbs. Site it toward the back of a sunny border where its tall, architectural form reads as a vertical accent, and let the foliage die back naturally once bloom finishes.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun; Purple Dynamite is a selection with unusually dark, glossy, almost black-purple florets.

directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun, since Fritillaria persica resents soggy ground, especially in summer dormancy. Purple Dynamite produces a tall spike of extremely dark, glossy purple florets that open sequentially from bottom to top above glossy green foliage, giving a bolder, more saturated color than the typical dusky-plum species. The stiff, upright flower spires make striking cut flowers and a strong vertical accent among spring bulbs such as daffodils, muscari, and tulips. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and avoid disturbing established clumps, which flower best left undisturbed for several years.

planting.note: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; this trade name (treated by some current taxonomies as a form of Colchicum speciosum) produces some of the largest flowers in the genus, with a white heart and orange anthers.

directions: Plant corms as soon as they become available in late summer, about 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Sold under this long-used trade name (closely allied with, and by some current taxonomies treated as a form of, Colchicum speciosum), it sends up broad, goblet-shaped, fragrant rosy-purple flowers directly from bare ground in early autumn, with a white heart and orange anthers, often eight or more flowers rising from a single large corm. The wide, glossy, strap-shaped leaves that follow the next spring must be left to die back naturally by early summer to recharge the corm, even though they can look coarse in a tidy border. Because every part of the plant is toxic if eaten, keep it out of reach of grazing pets or livestock, and pair it with later-emerging perennials that can mask the fading spring foliage.

planting.note: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Pleniflorum is a fully double, rosy-lilac sport of the common meadow saffron.

directions: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer, about 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Pleniflorum is a fully double sport of the common meadow saffron, producing many-petaled, rosy-lilac flowers that look almost like small peonies rising leafless from bare soil in early autumn, in contrast to the simple six-petaled cups of the wild species. The heavier double blooms are more prone to flopping after rain than single colchicums, so a site with light shade or shelter from deciduous trees helps keep them upright longer. Broad, strap-like leaves follow in spring and must be allowed to die back naturally by early summer to recharge the corm, so plant among later perennials that can hide the fading foliage. All parts are toxic if ingested, so avoid placing it near vegetable beds or grazing animals.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jeannine is a selection of golden garlic chosen for larger, more densely packed flower heads than the species.

directions: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Jeannine is a robust selection of golden garlic, producing rounded clusters of bright yellow, star-shaped flowers held above gray-green, strap-like foliage, with larger and more densely packed flower heads than the ordinary species. It spreads readily by offsets and self-seeding in congenial sites, naturalizing into broad patches under deciduous shrubs or in rock gardens where little else blooms in late spring. Once established it tolerates considerable summer drought and needs no routine care beyond letting the foliage yellow and wither naturally after bloom. Its compact size and cheerful color make it a good companion for blue-flowered spring bulbs such as grape hyacinth or dwarf iris.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sam Arnott is one of the largest-flowered and most vigorous classic snowdrop cultivars, prized also for its honey fragrance.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally under deciduous trees where they get bright light before the canopy leafs out. Sam Arnott is one of the largest-flowered and most reliably vigorous snowdrops in general cultivation, with rounded, honey-scented white blooms marked by a neat green blotch at the tip of the inner segments, held on sturdy stems that stand up well to late-winter weather. It bulks up into generous clumps faster than many named snowdrop cultivars, making it a good choice for gardeners who want a classic, dependable drift rather than a rare collector's item. Divide and move clumps in the green, right after flowering while the foliage is still active, for the most reliable transplant success, and always buy nursery-propagated bulbs rather than wild-collected stock.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Mount Everest is a tall, large-flowered selection of giant snowdrop with broad, gray-green foliage.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Mount Everest is a robust giant snowdrop selection, taller and larger-flowered than the common species, with broad, glaucous gray-green leaves and rounded white blooms marked by a green blotch at the base of the inner segments. Its extra vigor and bulk make it stand out in a winter border or naturalized drift even from a distance, unlike many smaller snowdrop cultivars that reward closer inspection. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulbs for the following year, and divide congested clumps in the green just after flowering if you want to spread the display. Buy only nursery-propagated bulbs, since wild collection has depleted native Galanthus elwesii populations in parts of its range.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Firmament is a compact ornamental onion with tight, deep violet-purple flower globes, shorter than Purple Sensation or Globemaster.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Firmament forms tight, densely packed spheres of small, deep violet-purple, star-shaped florets on sturdy stems noticeably shorter than most giant ornamental onions, making it easier to work into the middle of a mixed border without staking. It blooms in late spring, drawing bees in large numbers, and the dried seed heads hold their shape for weeks afterward, adding structure to the border long after the color fades. Once established, it tolerates considerable summer drought and needs little attention beyond letting the strappy foliage yellow and die back naturally after bloom. Interplant with later-emerging perennials to hide the foliage, which typically fades before or during flowering as is normal for ornamental onions.
